Bayesian spatiotemporal small-area analysis of COVID-19 vaccination coverage across Texas counties

Results report. The companion document, 01_source_inventory.md, lists every source, what was verified in it, and why the age group, time intervals and study period differ from the original proposal.

Throughout, recorded means a number taken from Texas DSHS records and a Census population estimate, and modelled means a posterior summary from the Bayesian model. Both describe vaccine receipt as recorded in the state registry. Neither measures willingness or acceptance.

1. Summary

What could be studied. The records support first-dose coverage of residents aged 16 and over (not 18 and over), for 254 counties, from 24 May 2021 to 9 May 2023, at the dates on which original DSHS workbooks survive. County counts before mid-April 2021 are incomplete in a county-specific way, so the first five months of the rollout enter only as the coverage each county had reached by 24 May 2021. Sixteen counties, most of them along the Mexican border, have more recorded vaccinated adults than adult residents; they are shown but not modelled. A separate extension, 03_early_rollout.md, reconstructs county coverage back to December 2020 under an explicit assumption about the recipients who had no county on record; it is kept apart because nothing in this report rests on that assumption.

Recorded coverage.

  • Statewide, recorded 16+ first-dose coverage rose from 52.5% on 24 May 2021 to 82.3% on 9 May 2023. In the 238 counties whose records can be read as resident coverage it rose from 50.9% to 77.2%.
  • The median county went from 41.3% to 61.9%, a gain of 20.6 percentage points.
  • The gaps between counties widened. The distance between the 90th- and 10th-percentile county grew from 21.7 to 26.2 points, and the standard deviation across counties from 8.4 to 10.8 points. Counties that were ahead in May 2021 gained more afterwards: each extra point of starting coverage went with 0.18 more points of later gain (95% confidence interval 0.11 to 0.24).
  • County ranks barely moved (rank correlation between start and end 0.90); 71% of the counties in the lowest fifth in May 2021 were still there in May 2023.

Modelled uptake among adults not yet vaccinated.

  • Pooled over the 238 counties, 8.4% of still-unvaccinated adults received a first dose per 30 days in the first interval (25 May to 22 June 2021). The rate peaked at 12.6% during the Delta wave (22 July to 21 August 2021), stayed near 5% through January 2022, and was at or below 1% from June 2022. The median county was always below the pooled rate (3.9% and 8.6% in the same two intervals) because the most populous counties vaccinated faster.
  • Uptake differed widely between counties: the rate in the 90th-percentile county was 3.0 times that in the 10th-percentile county. Rates were lowest in the Panhandle, the Rolling Plains and deep East Texas, and highest in the large metropolitan counties and South Texas. Counties with higher coverage in May 2021 also had higher uptake among their remaining unvaccinated adults afterwards (1.49 times higher per 10 points of starting coverage, 95% confidence interval 1.42 to 1.56), which is why the gaps widened.
  • Counties with a larger share of older adults had lower later uptake (hazard ratio 0.83 (0.78 to 0.88) per 6.2 points of the 65+ share). Counties with more reported cases in the previous 30 days had higher uptake (1.06 (1.03 to 1.09) per 4.0-fold higher case rate). Household income was positively associated with coverage reached by May 2021 (odds ratio 1.05 (1.01 to 1.10) per 27% higher income); its association with later uptake is 1.05 (0.98 to 1.13), an interval that includes no association.

Model checks.

  • Spatial structure lowered the prediction error for counties with no data by 14% when random counties were withheld and by 13% when whole regions were, compared with the same model without it.
  • Letting each county follow its own course over time (a mean-reverting process, model M4) lowered the error for a county's next interval by 8% and made the uncertainty intervals for later intervals better calibrated. It did not reduce the average error further ahead, and it made predictions for counties with no data 8% worse. No model was best at everything, so the report uses M4 for modelled uptake and the plain spatial model (M1) for statements about spatial structure. County results differ little between the two (median 0.5%).
  • No model forecast the statewide level of the next interval well: forecasts for the two intervals after the Delta-wave peak and for the Omicron wave were 1.5 to 5 points per 30 days too high.
  • Modelled uptake reproduces recorded uptake except in very small counties (median difference 0.002 points per 30 days in counties with more than 50,000 adults, 0.16 points below 5,000 adults). For 136 of 238 counties the county effect differs from its neighbours' with 95% posterior probability, so local differences are kept. A prediction from neighbours and predictors alone would miss a county's May 2023 coverage by 3.6 points on average.

Main cautions. Recorded coverage is a complete count, not a sample, so its uncertainty comes from the records and the population estimates, not from sampling, and the credible intervals do not cover it. Uptake among "adults not yet vaccinated" depends on a population estimate; where recorded coverage is high, a small error in that estimate is a large error in the number of people left. Associations are between county characteristics and county outcomes and say nothing about individuals.

2. What was analysed
Outcome Residents aged 16+ recorded with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, by county of residence
Source "By County, Age" sheet of original Texas DSHS "COVID-19 Vaccine Data by County" workbooks, recovered from the Internet Archive (40 usable editions)
Recorded coverage Count divided by the Census Bureau (Vintage 2025) estimate of residents aged 16+ on 1 July 2021
Uptake in an interval Adults newly recorded with a first dose, divided by adults not yet recorded as vaccinated at the start of the interval; reported per 30 days
Time grid Baseline 24 May 2021, then 12 intervals to 9 May 2023: nine of 26 to 35 days (to 25 February 2022), then 94, 174 and 170 days
Counties 254 described; 238 in the models
Predictors Share of adults aged 65+ (Census estimates, 2021); median household income (ACS 2019-2023); confirmed plus probable COVID-19 cases reported in the 30 days before each interval, per 100,000 residents (DSHS)
Neighbours Census county adjacency: 724 neighbouring pairs

The proposal asked for adults 18+, calendar months, and a study period chosen from the verified overlap. The inventory explains each change. In brief: the only 18+ county counts are in a CDC file that has no Texas data before 22 October 2021 and disagrees with DSHS by up to 36% in individual counties; DSHS's own age bands start at 16; and its workbooks survive only on the dates the Internet Archive captured them.

3. Recorded coverage

3.1 The rollout before the baseline

Statewide, the rollout before the baseline can be described by month from the last DSHS edition's count of first doses by date of vaccination. Everyone vaccinated in these months was 16 or older.

Month of vaccination First doses Texans 16+ with a first dose at month end (%) Uptake among those not yet vaccinated, per 30 days (%) Coverage the state reported at the time (%)
December 2020 514,176 2.2 3.7 1.5
January 2021 1,827,899 10.2 7.9
February 2021 1,703,270 17.5 8.8 15.5
March 2021 4,360,448 36.5 22.3 32.9
April 2021 3,194,801 50.3 21.8 48.1

Uptake among adults not yet vaccinated was 8-9% per 30 days in January and February 2021 and about 22% in March and April, as supply grew and eligibility widened (to everyone aged 16 and over from 29 March). The last column shows reporting lag: what the state had published by the first day of the following month was 0.8 to 3.5 points below what was eventually attributed to the month (no edition survives for 1 February 2021).

By county, no such description is possible without an assumption. Until the edition of 15 April 2021, 5-11% of recipients had no county on record, and the correction added 1% to Harris County's count but 19% to Tarrant's and 25% to Denton's (Figure 1). The extension 03_early_rollout.md makes the assumption explicit and follows the counties from the first doses.

3.3 Did the gaps between counties widen or narrow?

They widened (Figure 4, upper panel).

Records through 10th percentile 25th Median 75th 90th percentile Gap 90th - 10th (points) Standard deviation Pooled coverage
24 May 2021 32.23 36.33 41.27 47.25 53.95 21.73 8.42 50.86
23 Sep 2021 44.68 48.45 54.49 61.36 67.56 22.87 9.68 66.92
25 Feb 2022 49.86 54.46 60.21 67.89 74.23 24.37 10.34 74.18
30 May 2022 50.68 55.14 61.02 68.65 75.29 24.60 10.47 75.25
09 May 2023 51.33 55.89 61.91 70.37 77.57 26.24 10.82 77.22
  • The 10th percentile of county coverage rose by 19.1 points and the 90th percentile by 23.6.
  • Later gains were positively related to starting coverage (Figure 4, lower panel): slope 0.18 points per point, correlation 0.32.
  • In relative terms the divergence is larger. On 24 May 2021 the 10th-percentile county had 1.5 times the unvaccinated share of the 90th-percentile county (67.8% against 46.0%); on 9 May 2023 it had 2.2 times (48.7% against 22.4%).
  • The gap had reached 24.4 points by 25 February 2022 and was 26.2 points at the end.

A widening in percentage points is not automatic. If every county vaccinated the same share of its remaining unvaccinated adults, counties that started lower would gain more points and the gap would shrink. It grew because uptake among the unvaccinated was itself higher where coverage was already higher (section 4.4).

These 16 counties hold 8.8% of Texans aged 16+ but 35% of the adult first doses recorded statewide in January-February 2022 and 55% of those recorded between November 2022 and May 2023. Their counts keep rising long after they pass 100% of the population estimate. Fourteen of the 16 are in South Texas or along the Rio Grande; Reeves and Loving are in the far-west oil field. The records do not identify the recipients. A plausible reading, which these files cannot confirm, is that people who were not usual residents (cross-border patients, people held in custody, temporary workers) were recorded at local addresses. The counts are reported as recorded and are not interpreted as resident coverage. Statewide figures that include these counties (the "all counties" columns of the interval table) are inflated to an unknown degree for the same reason.

4. Modelled uptake

4.1 Model

For county i and interval k of length d days:

new first doses[i,k] ~ Binomial(adults not yet vaccinated[i,k], p[i,k])

log(-log(1 - p[i,k])) = log(d[k] / 30)
                        + intercept
                        + b_age * age[i] + b_income * income[i] + b_cases * cases[i,k]
                        + time[k]            shared time effect (random walk over interval midpoints)
                        + county[i]          county effect
                        + path[i,k]          county-specific course over time (models M2-M4)
                        + deviation[i,k]     county-interval deviation

The complementary log-log link with the interval length as an offset means that everything on the right-hand side describes the rate per 30 days at which still-unvaccinated adults are vaccinated (a hazard), whatever the length of the interval. Exponentiated coefficients are hazard ratios.

Model County effect County-specific course
M0 Independent across counties (no spatial structure) none
M1 BYM2: a spatially smooth part shared with neighbours plus an independent part none
M2 BYM2 a straight-line trend per county
M3 BYM2 a random walk per county, summing to zero over time (Knorr-Held type II)
M4 BYM2 a mean-reverting process per county in continuous time (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck)

The county-interval deviation absorbs variation beyond the binomial. Without it, counties with millions of residents would be treated as measured without error and would dictate every estimate. Predictors are standardised. Standard deviations have penalised-complexity priors with a 1% prior probability of exceeding 1 on the log-hazard scale; the BYM2 mixing parameter has prior probability two-thirds of being below 0.5. The models were fitted with R-INLA 26.08.07 (integrated nested Laplace approximation). Medians and 95% credible intervals of coefficients and variance parameters are quantiles of R-INLA's posterior marginals; those of quantities that combine several parameters (county rates, relative uptake, modelled change in coverage) come from 1,000 joint posterior draws. Partial pooling enters through the county effect, the county course and the deviation: where a county-interval has few events its estimate leans on the county's other intervals, its neighbours and its predictors, and where it has many the estimate follows the count.

A second, cross-sectional model describes the coverage each county had reached at the baseline (binomial, logit link, BYM2 county effect, the same age and income predictors, and cumulative reported cases before vaccination began on 14 December 2020).

4.2 Which model predicts best

Four out-of-sample experiments, each refitting the model with the tested county-intervals withheld:

  • A. Counties with no data. Ten random folds of counties; every interval of the held-out counties is predicted.
  • B. Regions with no data. Each of the eight DSHS public health regions is held out in turn, so most of a held-out county's neighbours are held out with it.
  • C. Later intervals. For a random half of the counties, every interval after an origin (21 August 2021, 20 November 2021 or 25 February 2022) is withheld while the other half stays observed. The statewide level of the later intervals is then known, and the test isolates what the model knows about each county's own course.
  • D. Next interval. Everything after an origin is withheld for all counties and the next interval is predicted, for nine origins. This is a true forecast.

The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures how far the whole predictive distribution lies from what was recorded, in percentage points of uptake per 30 days; lower is better. The log score is the log of the probability the prediction gave to the recorded count; higher is better, and it penalises a confident miss much more heavily than CRPS does. "Relative log-hazard correlation" is the correlation between predicted and recorded county positions within an interval, after removing whatever error all counties share. "End coverage" is coverage on 9 May 2023 computed from the predicted interval rates.

The statements below rest on differences between models scored on the same county-intervals. Counties with no data (A, B): spatial structure helps. With random counties withheld, the BYM2 model's CRPS is 0.77 against 0.89 for the non-spatial model (14% lower). Its 95% predictive intervals are narrower (6.4 against 7.5 points) and contain the recorded count as often (93.4% against 93.0%). It predicts a withheld county's coverage on 9 May 2023 to within 3.6 points on average, against 4.6. With whole regions withheld the CRPS advantage is 13% (0.80 against 0.92), but the model then says much less about which county in the region is ahead of which: the correlation between predicted and recorded county positions is 0.37, against 0.56 when only scattered counties are withheld.

County-specific courses cannot help a county that has no data. A straight-line trend per county (M2) leaves the CRPS where it was (0.77 in A, 0.81 in B). The mean-reverting course (M4) makes it 8% worse in experiment A (0.83) and 5% worse in experiment B (0.85). M4's intervals for an unseen county are wider (8.1 points against 6.4), because part of what sets a county apart is carried by its own course, which its neighbours cannot inform. Its CRPS stays below the non-spatial model's in both experiments (M4 minus M0: -0.059 (-0.130 to 0.004) in A and -0.076 (-0.135 to -0.023) in B), though in A the interval for that difference reaches zero.

Later intervals (C): county-specific courses help the next interval and the calibration, not the average error further ahead. Over all withheld intervals the CRPS is almost the same for every model: 0.42, 0.42, 0.42, 0.42 and 0.41 for M0 to M4. The difference is in the first withheld interval, where M4 scores 0.67 and M3 0.68 against 0.73 for M1 (M4 is 8% lower). Further ahead the county-specific courses bring no reduction in CRPS: M4 minus M1 is -0.001 (-0.012 to 0.009) two to three intervals ahead and 0.006 (0.000 to 0.011) four or more ahead.

What improves at every horizon is how honest the predictions are about their uncertainty. The log score is higher for all three models with county-specific courses (M4 minus M1: 0.135 (0.085 to 0.190)). Their 95% intervals contained the recorded count more often: 91.5% for M3, 90.6% for M4 and 89.6% for M2, against 87.5% for M1. All are below the nominal 95%, so every model is somewhat overconfident about later intervals. The intervals for coverage on 9 May 2023 contained the recorded figure for 89% of withheld counties with M3 and 88% with M4, against 79% with M1. The average error of that coverage prediction is nearly the same for every model (1.2 points for M4, 1.2 for M1). Spatial structure makes no difference in this experiment (M1 minus M0: -0.001 (-0.007 to 0.005) points of CRPS), because a county's own history is more informative than its neighbours.

M3 and M4 are close. M4 has the lower CRPS (M4 minus M3: -0.011 (-0.017 to -0.006)) and M3 the higher log score (-0.037 (-0.064 to -0.012)), which comes from intervals two or more steps ahead. For the next interval M4's CRPS is lower by an amount whose interval reaches zero (-0.008 (-0.017 to 0.000)), so the two are at most slightly apart there.

Next interval (D): no model forecasts the statewide level. CRPS is 1.12, 1.06, 1.05, 1.06 and 1.03 for M0 to M4, well above the one-interval-ahead error in experiment C (0.67 for M4), where the statewide level was known. Most of the excess comes from three of the nine forecasts, in which every model predicted too much uptake:

24 Sep 2021 - 25 Oct 2021 9.70 5.25 4.91 4.68 4.45 4.56 4.53
26 Oct 2021 - 20 Nov 2021 5.25 5.26 -0.46 -0.30 -0.30 -0.34 -0.25

22 Dec 2021 - 21 Jan 2022 5.14 5.37 -0.04 -0.05 0.00 -0.03 -0.07

The two intervals after the Delta-wave peak and the interval of the Omicron wave were forecast 1.5 to 5 points per 30 days too high. The models carry the last level forward, and nothing in them anticipates the end of a surge. The case-rate predictor does not help here: it describes differences between counties at the same time, and during the Omicron wave uptake halved while reported cases rose to their highest level. With only nine forecasts the differences between models are imprecise, and they do not repeat when the experiment is run again (next paragraph). M4 has the lowest CRPS, but its margin over M1 has an interval that includes zero (-0.025 (-0.076 to 0.017)), and no ranking of the models should be read from this experiment. The models still place counties correctly relative to one another: the correlation between predicted and recorded county positions in the next interval is 0.74 for M4 and 0.72 for M0.

How far these comparisons repeat. All four experiments were run again on 24 November 2026 (section 7). The mean CRPS of a model in an experiment changed by at most 0.027 points, or 2.6%. In experiments A, B and C, 124 of the 126 differences between models in the table above gave the same verdict as before (interval below zero, above zero, or including it). In experiment D only 12 of 20 did, so no ranking of the models should be read from experiment D.

Which model is used for what. No model is best at everything.

  • M4 is used for modelled uptake (sections 4.3 to 4.5). It has the lowest CRPS in experiment C, the best scores for a county's next interval, and the best leave-one-out score below. Those are the tests closest to what partial pooling has to do in this study: steady the estimate for a county-interval with few events by using the same county's other intervals. M3 is the close alternative, with better-calibrated predictions two or more intervals ahead and a slightly higher CRPS. M4 was preferred because it is at least as good at the nearest interval and each fit takes about one minute instead of about ten, which made it practical to refit it in every validation experiment and in the sensitivity analysis.
  • M1 is used for statements about spatial structure (the share of variance that is spatially structured, the right-hand map of Figure 8) and for the neighbours-only check in section 5. It is the simplest of the models that do best for counties with no data (M2 matches it there), and its county effect separates cleanly into a smooth part and an independent part.

The choice matters little for what is reported below. County relative uptake (section 4.4) computed from M3 instead of M4 differs by a median of 0.2% and by more than 2.0% in one county in twenty; the largest difference is 9% (King County, 198 adults). Computed from M1, the median difference is 0.5% and the largest 11% (King County, 198 adults). The predictor associations are similar in all five models (section 4.5). M3 was run only in experiments C and D, because of the time its fits take.

In-sample statistics separate the models poorly, because the county-interval deviation lets every model reproduce the data it was fitted to. WAIC differs by only 35 units in about 25,700 between the best and the worst model, and it puts M4 last. With about 1,600 effective parameters for 2,855 county-intervals WAIC is outside the range in which it is reliable, and what it measures here is mostly how well a model would predict a repeat count for the same county-interval with its deviation known, which every model does equally well. It is shown for completeness and was not used to choose a model. The leave-one-out measure (mean log conditional predictive ordinate, higher is better) withholds the county-interval itself. It puts M4 first and, like the log score in experiment C, puts the three models with county-specific courses ahead of the two without. R-INLA flagged its leave-one-out approximation as unreliable for 44 county-intervals under M3 and 10 under M2, against 1 under M4, so the M2 and M3 values are less secure.

4.3 Uptake over time

Figure 6. Uptake per 30 days among adults not yet vaccinated: all 238 counties pooled, the median county with the 10th-90th percentile range, and counties grouped by their coverage at baseline.

Pooled over the 238 counties, the rate fell from 8.4% per 30 days (25 May to 22 June 2021) to 6.0%, doubled to 12.6% from 22 July to 21 August 2021 as the Delta wave arrived, and eased to 9.7% and then to about 5% for the four intervals from late September 2021 to late January 2022. It was 2.7% from 22 January to 25 February 2022, 1.3% to 30 May 2022, 1.0% to 20 November 2022 and 0.5% to 9 May 2023.

The typical county was well below the pooled rate throughout. The modelled median county ran at 3.9% in the first interval and 8.6% at the peak, when the 10th- and 90th-percentile counties were at 5.5% and 13.4%. In every interval the third of counties with the highest coverage at baseline also had the highest uptake rate among their remaining unvaccinated adults (Figure 6, lower panel).

Figure 7. Recorded and modelled uptake in six counties, with 95% credible intervals.

Figure 7 shows what the model adds to the records. In Harris County the modelled rate equals the recorded one and its interval is too narrow to see. In King County, with 198 adults, one first dose moves the recorded rate by more than half a percentage point; the modelled rate follows the county's general level and its interval is wide.

4.4 Where uptake was higher or lower

Figure 8. Modelled uptake relative to the average county (left, model M4) and the spatially smooth part of the county effect that the predictors do not explain (right, model M1).

Figure 9. The 12 highest and 12 lowest counties, with 95% credible intervals.

Figure 8 (left) maps each county's modelled uptake rate relative to the average county, averaged over the 12 intervals. The 10th-percentile county is at 0.61 and the 90th-percentile county at 1.80, a 3.0-fold difference. For 113 of the 238 counties the 95% credible interval lies wholly below 1 and for 93 wholly above. The six most populous counties are all above the average county (Harris 3.1, Dallas 2.5, Tarrant 1.7, Bexar 3.7, Travis 3.1, Collin 2.2). The lowest county is Newton at 0.30 (0.27 to 0.32) and the highest La Salle at 4.72 (4.29 to 5.21). Several of the highest are small South Texas counties next to flagged ones (La Salle, Zavala, Jim Hogg), where non-resident recipients may also be present.

Starting coverage and later uptake go together: across the 238 counties the correlation between coverage on 24 May 2021 and modelled relative uptake afterwards is 0.73, and uptake was 1.49 times higher per 10 points of starting coverage (95% confidence interval 1.42 to 1.56, from the scatter between counties). This describes these counties; it is not adjusted for the three predictors.

The right-hand map shows the part of the county effect that is spatially smooth and not explained by the three predictors. In the model without county-specific courses (M1), 70% of the between-county variance left after the predictors is of this spatially structured kind (posterior median and 95% credible interval 0.70 (0.49 to 0.87)). The standard deviation of the county effect is 0.37 (0.33 to 0.42) on the log scale: a county at the 97.5th percentile of that effect has 4.2 times the uptake rate of one at the 2.5th percentile with the same predictors. Coverage reached by 24 May 2021 was spatially structured to a similar or greater degree: in the baseline model the structured share of the county effect is 0.82 (0.59 to 0.95).

Counties also drift around their own level. In M4 the county-specific course has a standard deviation of 0.43 (0.39 to 0.47) and a half-life of 5.8 months (95% CrI 4.4 to 7.7): a county running above its usual level is, on average, half as far above it that much later.

So the spatial pattern is real (Moran's I of the county effects from the non-spatial model is 0.48), and neighbours are informative, but neighbours alone would hide persistent local differences of several points of coverage. 6. What the credible intervals cover, and what they do not

Recorded coverage is observed. The registry is meant to hold every dose given to a county's residents, so recorded coverage is a complete count rather than an estimate from a sample. It has no sampling error and is reported without intervals. The model does not improve on it; for the cumulative change in coverage over the study the modelled and recorded figures differ by a median of 0.03 points across counties (largest difference 3.7 points).

What the model's intervals include: chance variation in the number of first doses given a county's underlying rate; uncertainty about that rate where numbers are small; uncertainty in the county, time and county-course effects, in the predictor coefficients and in the variance parameters.

What they leave out:

  • Errors in the counts. After April 2021, 1.2% to 3.0% of first-dose recipients statewide have no county. A few percent of each interval's doses are reported late and land in the next interval. Record corrections move small numbers between counties. Recipients who are not residents are counted where they were recorded. Doses given by federal agencies may be missing: CDC's count for Bell County (Fort Hood) is 36% above DSHS's. As a general check, CDC's 18+ coverage and DSHS's 16+ coverage, computed on the same population estimates, agreed closely across the modelled counties on 26 October 2021 (correlation 0.97, median absolute difference 1.4 points, more than 5 points apart in 11 counties). By 9 May 2023 they agreed less well (rank correlation 0.93, median absolute difference 1.7 points, more than 5 points apart in 26 counties and more than 10 in 11).
  • Errors in the population estimates. The denominator is an estimate for one date, 1 July 2021. The numerator keeps people who later died or moved away and misses doses that newcomers received elsewhere, and DSHS appears to classify people by age at vaccination while the population ages.
  • Model form. Other reasonable models would give somewhat different intervals.

Why denominator error matters most where coverage is high. The number of adults "not yet vaccinated" is the population estimate minus the recorded count. A 3% error in the population estimate changes that number by 6% when recorded coverage is 50%, by 12% at 75% and by 30% at 90%. Uptake rates for high-coverage counties late in the study are therefore the least reliable numbers in this report, and county-intervals starting at 95% or more were not modelled at all.

The data do not settle whether income is associated with later uptake.
  • Flagged counties. Keeping them until their recorded coverage reaches 95% (S4) moves the income ratio to 1.01 (0.94 to 1.09) and raises the standard deviation of the county effect, which is what counties that do not behave like the rest would do.

7. Limitations

  • Sixteen counties and 8.8% of adults are outside the models, including El Paso, Hidalgo, Cameron and Webb. Conclusions about gaps and associations are about the other 238 counties.
  • The first five months of the rollout are not modelled in this report. They are represented by coverage on 24 May 2021. A county series for December 2020 to May 2021 needs an assumption about where the then-unassigned recipients lived; 03_early_rollout.md builds one, tests it and shows how little of its conclusions depends on it. One of its findings bears on section 4.5: the negative association with the share of older adults begins in April 2021, when eligibility opened to all adults.
  • Adults means 16 and over, the youngest adult band in the records.
  • Intervals are unequal and three are long. Month-level detail after February 2022 is not recoverable from the surviving files.
  • Counties with large institutions. A prison, military base or university puts people in the population estimate whose vaccinations may be recorded elsewhere or by another system, which lowers recorded coverage. The records cannot separate this from real differences in uptake. The CDC comparison suggests it matters in places: CDC's count is 36% above DSHS's in Bell County (Fort Hood) and 24% above in Live Oak County, one of the counties that differs most from its neighbours.
  • Reported cases changed character on 1 January 2022 (final counts before, provisional daily reports after), omit home tests, and reflect testing as well as infection.
  • Three predictors only. Age composition and income are correlated with rurality, health-care access, political preference and ethnic composition, none of which is in the model. The coefficients describe which counties had higher uptake, not why.
  • Refitting does not give identical numbers. R-INLA does not return exactly the same fit twice on the same computer, and the 1,000 posterior draws then come out as a different sample even though their seed is fixed. When the models of sections 4 and 6 and of the extension were fitted again on 24 November 2026, hazard ratios changed by at most 0.0013, county relative uptake by at most 1.2% (its interval bounds by at most 2.9%) and modelled uptake in a county and interval by at most 0.20 points per 30 days. Of the 510 values that the scripts fill into this report and the extension from the fitted models and the records, 29 came out differently, each by at most 5 units in its last printed digit; they are listed in rerun_changed_values.csv. The out-of-sample experiments of section 4.2 were run again as well. Of the 373 values quoted from them, 192 came out differently: the mean scores (CRPS) changed by at most 0.027 points, or 2.6%, and section 4.2 says which comparisons between models held. The numbers printed here are those of one run, and the last digit of a modelled number should be read with that in mind. Recorded coverage and everything computed from it repeat exactly. The comparison is made by R/18_rerun_check.R.
  • Approximate inference. R-INLA approximates the posterior. A second approximation strategy gave the same estimates (variant S12), but no simulation-based (MCMC) fit was run to confirm them.

8. Reproducing and tracing results

README.md lists the commands. Every raw file is in data/raw/ with its address and SHA-256 in data/raw/MANIFEST.csv. The numbers in this report's tables are produced by R/10_report_tables.R from the CSV files in outputs/tables/; the figures and their data by R/08_outputs.R.
